utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Case Manager Sebastiaan van Hooydonk, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Denis Stoychev, Simon Levett, and appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Miroslav Cuskic, and Elayne Hannon, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jovicinac, would you please confirm that you are seeing and hearing us from your facilities in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Registrar from the field office in Belgrade. I hope you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you try again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Registrar from the field office in Belgrade. I hope can you hear me now. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Would the Court Officer please, first of all, invite Mr. Jovicinac to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That solemn declaration imposes upon you an obligation to speak the truth and should you fail to do so, there are penalties which attach to your giving false or misleading testimony. On behalf of the Tribunal, I thank you for coming to agree to testify to the Tribunal, and we are receiving you, of course, by way of videolink from Belgrade. The -- it is expected that your testimony would be completed within the course of today, and the procedure of the Tribunal is that there are breaks to allow the -- for technical reasons but should you for any reasons need to take a break, if you would indicate that to us, we would, of course, accommodate you. The questioning on behalf of the Chamber at whose instances you are called, will be led by Judge Harhoff, who -- to whom the camera will soon switch and he sits at my left. He will begin the questioning, and I will now pass over to him so that he will ask the preliminary questions of you and then we would launch in your testimony. Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: My name is Srboljub Jovicinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is the date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: 24 January 1949. I was born in the village of Vrucinic in the Novi Pazar municipality, in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Jovicinac, what was your professional education?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I finished primary school in the village of Vrucinic, and, after that, I went to secondary textile technology school at Novi Pazar. Then I went to Banja Luka -- secondary military school in Banja Luka. After secondary school, I enrolled in law school and graduated in Banja Luka. I'm a lawyer, and I passed my bar exam, and I have some modest experience in the judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us, when did you graduate from law school?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I graduated in 1986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what was your occupation in 1992? And what is it today?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: In 1992, from August on, I was employed by the basic military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. And some two months or so later, I was appointed deputy military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what did you do before August 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Before August 1992, I worked in Sarajevo for a while at the 7th Army Command as a desk clerk in the military ombudsman's office. After that, I returned to Banja Luka. I was appointed secretary of the second-instance housing commission of the 5th Banja Luka Corps. From there, I went on to the training centre, but I couldn't give you the exact date. I forgot it. There, I was a desk clerk for legal affairs at the armoured units training centre, and I was also a teacher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So, if I understand you correctly, you began to work in August 1992 at the military prosecutor's office in Banja Luka. And then, a couple of months later, which would have been in October perhaps, you were then appointed deputy military prosecutor in Banja Luka. That is correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Jovicinac, have you ever testified before this Tribunal or before any other domestic court in relation to the events that took place during the war?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I have never testified before this Tribunal, but I was summoned as a witness to the District Court of Banja Luka to give evidence in a trial which, I suppose, is finished by now. I don't know how important it is to inform you that I had frequent contacts with the investigators of the OTP when they stayed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Or, more precisely, in the region where I had responsibility or jurisdiction as a prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, let me tell you, then, a bit about the procedures that will take place for -- during your testimony here today. First of all, as the Presiding Judge just told you, you have been called to testify by the Trial Chamber. That is to say, that you are not a witness of the Prosecution, nor of the Defence. The reason why we have called you is that we have heard almost all of the evidence in this trial against Mr. Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. I don't know if can you see the courtroom, but they would be seated to your left. And the reason we have called you is that we are sitting back with a few questions regarding the authority to --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- investigate and prosecute reserve and active-duty members of the police force for crimes committed during resubordination to the army. So this is main purpose of your testimony today, to clarify a few of these questions. We have assigned about one hour to the Chamber itself to put its questions to you, after which you will be cross-examined first by the Prosecution - and, again, if can you see the courtroom, they would be sitting to the right - and, thereafter, the two Defence parties have been given, all together, also one and a half hours. This runs up to, all together, four hours for today. And we hope that we can finish your testimony here before the end of the morning session, at a quarter to 2.00. The proceedings run for 90 minutes at a time, after which we have to have a break because the tapes, the videotapes that record these hearings, have to be changed. And during and after the cross-examination of the parties, the Judges may, at all times, also put questions to you. As you know, you have been accorded video testimony from Belgrade for good reasons, and -- but I just wanted to add to this that if at any point you need to have a break, or you have questions to us, or to the parties, then please do not hesitate to indicate this to the Registrar, who is sitting next to you, and we will accommodate you accordingly. And, lastly, Mr. Jovicinac, you must speak slowly and distinctly. Please listen carefully to the questions and try and answer them as concisely as you can. And especially when the Defence counsels will be cross-examining you, there's a risk of overlap because you both speak the same language. So, if you can, please observe a little pause between the questions asked to you by the counsel and your response to them. So that's all. Do you have a question -- any question at this point, Mr. Jovicinac?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let's get on with it then. My first question to you, Mr. Jovicinac, is about the military court in Banja Luka. When was the military court established? And can you tell us about the personal jurisdiction that the military court had; that is to say, over whom could it exercise its authority?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: The military court in Banja Luka and the military prosecutor's office, too, were established pursuant to an Assembly decision that was taken in August 2002 [as interpreted]. Neither the military court, nor the military prosecutor's office starting working immediately because much time was required to find personnel and I can state with almost full certainty that the first activities began only in late September. As for the jurisdiction of the military court, under the laws that were in force then, the military court had jurisdiction over all criminal offences, the perpetrators of which were members of the military. It also had jurisdiction over criminal offences involving prisoner of war as perpetrators of crimes. It had exclusive jurisdiction - I mean the military court in Banja Luka but also other military courts - over criminal offences against the armed forces, as well as criminal offences from chapter 15 which are -- is about the security of the country and defence. There was also a criminal offence from Article 136, if my memory serves me well, and that was in chapter 16, about conspiracy to commit criminal offences from chapter 15, as well as criminal offences against the armed forces, that would be chapter 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get into more detail about that in just a second. Can I, just for the accuracy of your testimony, mention that on page 7 of the testimony at line 4, you were quoted to say that the military court in Banja Luka was established pursuant to an Assembly decision taken in August 2002. I assume that the answer was that it was taken in August 1992. Can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, do you remember when the military court heard its first case?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I don't think I can give you a reliable answer now. The military court is an independent institution, as everybody knows. As a prosecutor, I didn't interfere with their business. But, as far as I remember, the first on-site investigations and the first actions were taken in September after manning, after issuing decisions on appointments. But I believe that even these decisions date from September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. This is very helpful. Mr. Jovicinac, as we are going to dwell a bit on the law, I suggest that we have a look at some of the relevant provisions. And could ask the Registrar to call up Exhibit P1284.07, which, I hope, is the Law on Military Courts from December 1976. And if we could go to Article 13. I think that would be on page 2 of the English version. Sir, do you have before you Article 13 of the Law on the Courts -- on Military Courts in -- in a language that you can understand? I see you're nodding, so I take it that you answer in the affirmative. Let's have a look at Article 13 or maybe even before. Let's start with Article 12, which is the preceding article. And Article 12 reads that military courts can try cases involving criminal acts committed by military personnel, and also cases involving criminal acts committed by other persons, and those other persons are then further specified in Article 13. If we go to Article 13, we see that military courts can try civilians as well for a particular number of crimes. And those crimes are then listed up in the criminal law, which is Exhibit L11, I believe, in the law library. If we could call up that document and find Article 114. Very well. Mr. Jovicinac, do you have the criminal law in front of you, and can you see Article 114?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. If the Registrar would assist us in going through these articles rapidly, then the first thing we see is that Article 114 deals with attack on the constitutional order. And Article 115 deals with acceptance of capitulation and occupation. And if we turn to the next page, we see that Article 116 deals with attack on the territorial integrity. Article 117 deals with attacks on the independence of the states. Article 118 is about prevention of the struggle against the enemy. Article 119 is about service in the enemy armed forces. Article 120 is providing assistance to the enemy. Article 121 is about weakening the military and defence strength. Article 122 deals with assassination of representatives of the highest state organs. And so on and so forth. This goes on right until Article 156. Now this would imply that military courts can try these crimes even if they were committed by civilians. But, sir --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- could you tell us if there is any legal basis in these instruments for the military prosecutors to investigate crimes allegedly committed by civilians other than these crimes which are directed against the security and integrity of the state? Could you, as military prosecutor, investigate and prosecute a civilian who had committed, say, a war crime against a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: A military prosecutor could launch an investigation against a civilian who committed war crimes but if he did it in complicity with a member of the military. These crimes are explicitly listed as being under the jurisdiction of military courts, and the prosecutor's office is linked to the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Maybe we could go back to the Law on Military Court and have a look at that provision again. If the Registrar could find Exhibit P1284.07 for us again.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: That's 12 and 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. And we will proceed to Article 14 and 15 as well. Very well. Mr. Jovicinac, do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. And if we could have the English version up on the screen as well of the rest of Article 13 and Article 14 and 15. Now, sir, you told us just now that the military courts could also prosecute a civilian who committed a war crime if that war crime was committed together with a member of the armed forces. Where do you find that provision; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the case of connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. And in which provision do you find the connection?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I -- I can't find my bearings in this particular section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Look at Article 13 in the penultimate paragraph. Is that the provision that we're looking for?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the provision. However, in the first part of the paragraph, it speaks about the civilians employed by the army. And then it says crimes committing during service or in relation with the service as well as for any other criminal acts that may be committed as -- by them as co-perpetrators or accomplices to servicemen. If I may be of assistance, if military courts have exclusive jurisdiction over military personnel, then other perpetrators who act as co-perpetrators, then the military court also has the jurisdiction to act in such instances as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you're right. Now, what if a civilian who was -- let's take the example of a policeman, for instance. We know from the evidence in this trial that quite frequently police forces would be resubordinated for a certain period of time to the army, to assist the army in combat operations. If a resubordinated policeman commits a war crime while he is taking part in the operation together with soldiers of the army, who would then be authorised and competent to try this policeman?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a very delicate question. I would like to refer you to the provision of the Law on the Service in the Military - I don't know exactly which provision that is - in which the command is based on the principle of unity of command, or singleness of command, as well as on the principles of subordination and singleness of command. To simplify it, that would mean that all subordinates are obliged to carry out all the orders issued by superiors. The Law on Courts is always an explicit one. Military courts try military personnel for the crimes committed by them. There is no provision in the law, nor did I have an opportunity to encounter that in practice. The case law or the law have managed to draw a line between these two issues. On the one hand, you have a norm which says that the military court can only try military personnel who committed criminal offences. On the other hand, you have a policeman who does not have the status of a member of the military. So I cannot give you an explicit answer that it would be the military court who would have the jurisdiction to try a policeman who committed a crime. However, if he did that as an accomplice of a member of the military, I can tell you, without hesitation, that it would be under the jurisdiction of the military court. However, if we are talking solely about a civilian policeman, I really wonder whether the military court can act. And I think that in such instances, a military prosecutor would declare himself disqualified because for any other structures other than the military the civilian courts have jurisdiction. Now, we have a situation that we have policemen who have been resubordinated. Its duty is to carry out the orders from the superior command in compliance with all the provisions governing the use of units raises a question which, in my view, hasn't been resolved either in the case law or in the legislature. What I see as an important thing in such situation where you have a combination of police and armed forces, if a crime is committed and detected immediately and reported immediately, and if you have a civilian mechanism initiated in terms of investigation or placing people in custody, then that's a mechanism that cannot be stopped anymore. However, as I said, I have some reservations whether this could be processed by a military court. To tell you the truth, I, as a military prosecutor, would prefer to defer this kind of cases to the prosecutors who have jurisdiction over the crimes committed by other individuals than those --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There is an error in transcript. It's page 13, line 6, because witness says something else. He said -- [Interpretation] In Serbian he said -- and if he can repeat. He said that: Even if I, as a military prosecutor, would submit a request, the military court would declare itself not to have the jurisdiction. So if you could please clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, unfortunately, you interrupted the translation of what the witness was saying. I think you should try to avoid that. Now we have an incomplete translation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, I'm sorry for this interruption. But interpretation is a difficult thing, and if the parties or the witnesses speak too fast, overlap, then it is very difficult for the interpreters to catch up. Now, Mr. Jovicinac, could you please repeat what you said about your inclination in case you were put before a -- a instance in which a civilian policeman who had been resubordinated to the army would come under your jurisdiction or not.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If we are to go now into more details, let me tell you that if I receive a criminal report, and if I am to carry out a serious check of the allegations contained therein, pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure, I have to find out whether this police unit was really resubordinated to the army, whether it was placed under the military command, and if the criminal report undoubtedly shows that he had committed a crime, as a prosecutor, in view of the explicit norm from the Law on Military Courts and their jurisdiction, I would defer it to the jurisdiction of civilian courts. If I made a mistake and launched investigation before a military court, my view is -- and I'm quite sure that in that instance the military court would declare itself to have no jurisdiction and would defer the case to civilian courts because it involved a civilian policeman, and this is in line with the law governing the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. But please tell us the logic in this because it would perhaps seem logic that if a civilian policeman is resubordinated to the army, then, for the sake of the unity of the command, he is under the authority of the commanding officer of the army for the purpose of the military operation. Would it then not be logical to assume that this policeman would also fall under the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor, if he committed a crime during the time in which he was resubordinated to the army? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The military prosecutor would have jurisdiction to act against a civilian policeman for crimes that are exclusively within the jurisdiction of military courts. War crime does not fall into the category of exclusive jurisdiction of military courts. Now, what I see as an obstacle here, and I might have different views or maybe I can agree with your line of thinking, but the law is very clear here because every resubordination lasts for a limited duration of time. It's not a permanent status because status here is the decisive factor in determining the jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That seems logical, indeed. But if a civilian policeman is resubordinated to the army, even for a limited duration of time, then why wouldn't he have the same status as his brother in the army?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: You know, that would mean that I would then embark on an area that I'm not very familiar with. It was never a case that individuals were resubordinated but, rather, units as a whole, and every unit had its own superior commander who reported to a military commander. There is logic in affording this status to such personnel, but this is not provided in the law. And you know that we must act in compliance with the law. I am quite sure that if such a person would appeal such a proceedings, that these appeals would be accepted on the basis of wrongful jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that appeals were made to the -- to the military court or to the civilian courts?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: To the military court, of course. But the decision would be made by the supreme military court, not the one who conducted the proceedings. If I requested an investigation with the basic military court, the accused has a right to appeal such a decision taken by an investigating judge, and then the chamber would decide upon them. And if we strictly adhere to the provision from Article 13 from the Law on Military Courts, then this appeal, in my view, would be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the results of that appeal, in your opinion, would be that the military supreme court would defer the case to the civilian judiciary. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. The military court who conducted the proceedings would be -- would proceed it to the supreme military court. And then if we have a clash of jurisdictions, then it would be the supreme court who would render a final decision. That is stipulated by the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Thanks for this clarification. Let me move to some --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I may add just one more thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Errors may occur in the course of the proceedings, but there is always a higher instance that can remedy these mistakes in the previous proceedings. So, as far as I can remember, we had not had such a situation in our practice, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Speaking about practice --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just noticed that his answer to your last question was a little bit ambiguous. You put the proposition to him on appeal would the case be determined by -- I assume the supreme military court to defer a case against a civilian police officer and then he, I think, was confused about the issue of whether you meant the basic military court or the supreme court. So his answer "no," is, in that context, a bit ambiguous, at least the way I read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I thought I understood it correctly. But let's go back to the question again. Mr. Jovicinac, there's some uncertainty about the answer that you just gave to me. The question was this: If a civilian policeman who is resubordinated to the army for a limited period of time, and during his resubordination he commits a war crime, and for that war crime he is prosecuted by the military prosecutor but he appeals - he is unhappy with the decision of the military court - and he claims he should have been tried by the civilian court and he therefore appeals the jurisdiction of the military court to the supreme military court, then what, in your view, would the response for the decision made by the military supreme court?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If the supreme military court upholds the -- the appeal of the accused, it would annul the decision of the first-instance investigative magistrate and return the case to the first-instance military court for it to defer it to the civilian court that has jurisdiction. Furthermore, if that case -- sorry, that court that was seized with the case did not agree with that, then -- that is, in case of a clash of jurisdiction, then a higher court would have to be the one that decides in such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope it has become clearer now. Let's move to some of the practice. Did you ever have the opportunity to prosecute active-duty or reserve policemen who had been resubordinated to the army for any crimes committed during their resubordination? Was such a case ever put to you?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there was one such case, or two. I'm not fully certain. But we were not aware of their resubordination. It has been a long time, but if I remember correctly, an offence was committed outside the unit; that is, when the perpetrator was not with the unit. I cannot be more price now. But there was one such case, or maybe two. I remember that I -- I did not agree with the legal qualification of the offences and deferred it to the prosecutor's office that had jurisdiction. They accepted to investigate the case and acted upon my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure I fully understood your example. Were you talking about an incident in which a person who turned out to be a civilian policeman had committed a crime just outside the premises, and the case was then put before you, but you deferred the case back to the civilian prosecutor? Was that what the example was about?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: The offence was committed outside the context of combat. It was not a combat context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. Let's have a look at a few incidents in which, I believe, that you were involved. If the Registrar would be good enough to call up Exhibit 2D42 on the screen, please. Mr. Jovicinac, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is a dispatch issued by the deputy military prosecutor in Banja Luka, one Mr. Zoran Babic, dated 8th of March, 1993, concerning a case in which 12 suspects had been detained regarding a massacre of 80 civilians in the school of Velagici near Kljuc. Do you recall the incident?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if any of the 12 suspects who are listed here were policemen who had been resubordinated to the army?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What is your answer? You don't know; or do you know that they were not?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I have no such information. Judging by their personal information, they were all military conscripts serving with the Military Post number 4630, Kljuc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Now, a military conscript or, as the English translation goes, a military recruit, could that be a policeman who had been resubordinated? Is that how you would list a resubordinated policeman?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: A military prosecutor can give a description in such a document based on the description that he received in the criminal complaint. He merely relates the information contained therein. If the criminal report had qualified somebody as a civilian police officer, it would have been mentioned here. And that person would certainly have been tried, together with everybody else, because he, in that case, would be a co-perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. My interest was, rather, to be able to determine whether, by the description of these gentlemen, one could determine their -- their -- their provenance. If you take, for instance, the suspect number two, Mr. Krcmar, he is listed as a military recruit, and then his father and mother's name are mentioned. Could Mr. Krcmar be a resubordinated policeman, judging by the description of him here?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If I may read it all out, all the details. It says: "Ilija Krcmar, military recruit, father Gojko, mother Mila, born in Jajce, on 3 March 1967, permanently residing in Kljuc at 92 Josipa Broza Street, student by occupation, currently military conscript with Military Post 4630, Kljuc." This does not allow for the conclusion that he is a police officer, and it explicitly states that he was a student by occupation. He was also a member of a military unit. And the accused would certainly complain in the course of the proceedings, and the investigative judge would change this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at another incident. If the Registrar could pull up for us a document which has the English ERN number 03056945 and the following two pages. In B/C/S, it is ERN number 02063512 and also with the next two pages up until -3514.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Sorry, Your Honours. Please repeat the B/C/S ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this is document that I was looking for. What we have on the screen is 65 ter 2069. That would be the next document. So let's just stay with what the document -- with the document we have on the screen. And, Mr. Jovicinac, do you have it in B/C/S in front of you? You do. Have you seen the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall this incident? The document is a decision issued on 6 December 1992 by the investigating judge at the Banja Luka Military Court to remand in custody for one month four persons who all seem to be related - they all carry the name Gvozden - regarding an incident of the murder of eight Croat men and women that took place on the previous day in the village of Sasina. Do you remember the incident?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I remember this incident. This was the first serious case that the military prosecutor's office received, although I wasn't a prosecutor at the time, I was deputy. But I think I was present during the interrogation of one or two of these accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: They --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Jovicinac, if, to your recollection, any of the four accused, or suspects as they were at this time, were active-duty or reserve members of the civilian police who had been resubordinated to the army when they killed the eight Croat men and women in Sasina?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, to be completely honest, I don't remember that detail. I think that all of them or somebody was a member of the military. But the investigative judge didn't include this information. There is no criminal report because we could tell then, so we don't know their status. If possibly one of them was a police officer, then, due to the status of the others, if they were members of the military, then this police officer would also be included in the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We just have time enough to see if we, once again, could try and pull up the other incident that I was talking about. Mr. Registrar, can you find ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, there's a problem relating to the translation of this document. So what I would do instead is just to remind you of the incidents and ask you if you can recall it. It was about the killing of a Croat priest from November 1992 where three persons kidnapped and killed a Croat priest in a mine outside the village of Donja Ravska. Do you recall the incident?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If it has to do with Priest Matanovic [phoen], I really don't know much about the case, but there were some government organisations and international organisations that came to see me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, this incident from November 1992 was the killing of a Croat priest called Ivan Grgic. If you cannot recall, then please just tell us.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember. Our prosecutor's office may have investigated, but I really cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just contacted by the our Legal Officer to determine whether we should enter document 65 ter 2069 into evidence, but I don't see the use of it. We have the witness's testimony on record, and I would not seek to tender or to have this document admitted into evidence. Mr. Jovicinac, I thank you very much. At ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Judge Delvoie has an additional question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, you told us that you -- you would -- or the military prosecution would refer cases about crimes committed by resubordinated policemen to the civil authorities because - and I -- it was about a particular case. Because the offence, you said, was committed outside the context of combat. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That raises the question whether the answer would -- would have been different, whether, in other words, the military jurisdiction would be competent if crimes would have been committed in the context of combat. Let's take a hypothetical example of members of a resubordinated police unit, while in combat on the front line, kill a group of elderly women and young children who were seeking shelter in the basement of a village house. So clearly in the context of combat. Would you say that this would be something that would stay within the military jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, initially I provided an answer to such a question, a similar question, actually. If the offence was committed in co-perpetration with members of the military, then the military court would have exclusive jurisdiction. However, if they committed the offence, and if they were exclusively police officers, then I see no possibility for the military court to -- to deal with the case simply because the perpetrators did not have the status of members of the military. There is some logic to it, but, of course, the law has precedence over logic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, we've reached the point where we would take our first break. We will resume in 20 minutes, when the Prosecution - thanks - would be invited to put any questions to you arising out of the questions that the Tribunal has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do I take it from what I see on the screen that the witness has not yet resumed his seat? Could the Court Officer please confirm this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will deal with the -- this procedure by the -- very briefly, and then you can have the witness back before the camera. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just for the record, Mr. Hannis has now been replaced by Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Olmsted. The Chamber has been notified of the joint request by the parties for additional time for the examination of the Chamber witnesses Lisica and Kovac. The Chamber has considered this matter and decided that the times for Lisica will remain the same as determined in the Trial Chamber's scheduling order of the 15th of February. With regard to Witness Kovac, the Trial Chamber has decided to schedule an additional hearing on Friday, the 9th of March. The Prosecution will have one extra court session for the examination of this witness, and the Defence will jointly have another session for the examination of Kovac. The Friday's session will end at 12.05. Thank you. So, Mr. Court Officer, you can have the witness back before the camera. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, welcome back. I would now invite Mr. Olmsted, counsel for the Prosecution, to put such questions as he has to you. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovicinac.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Good morning. Greetings to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I first just want to ask you a question about your background. Can you confirm that you were appointed military prosecutor for the 1st Krajina Corps in May of 1993 and that you held that position until 1996?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have P1284.6 on the screen. This is tab number 7, Mr. Jovicinac, in your binder. And I'm interested in decision number 169, which is a RS Presidency decision on the establishment, seat and jurisdiction of the military courts and military prosecutors' offices. Can you confirm that it's this -- this is the decision that established the military courts and military prosecutors' offices?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived in the military prosecutor's office in August 1992, there was already a military prosecutor in that office; isn't that correct? There was a Spasoje Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasoje Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to confirm, he was already functioning as the military prosecutor when you arrived in the office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, in August and September, we had the process of establishing the prosecutor's office, procuring equipment, recruiting staff, appointing staff, et cetera. Real serious work started sometime toward the end of September, if I remember correctly, after such a long time. And I believe that first investigations were conducted in late September or early October. But I'm just relying on my memory. I cannot give you a decisive answer after such a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for that. But that's not my question. My question simply was that the military prosecutor, Mr. Pisarevic, he was already at the office when you joined the office; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm fully because I don't remember a decree issued to that effect. But everybody knew that he was going to be appointed to that post because the decision was made in that month. However, one cannot say whether the whole procedure can be conducted within the months starting from the decree and his essential assumption of duties. I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's have on the screen L51. Mr. Jovicinac, this will be tab 12 in your binder. And this is the RS Law on the Army, from June 1992. Sir, during your testimony, you mentioned that the military courts had jurisdiction over persons who were members of the army, as defined by law. And I want to draw your attention to Article 3 of this law which appears to define who are members of the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you confirm: If a person does not fall within this definition, then the military did not have criminal jurisdiction over that person, unless, of course, that person committed one of the crimes enumerated in Article 13?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you confirm that this definition does not include civilian police who have been resubordinated to the military?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. This definition does not include civilian police because the establishment of civilian police is regulated by the Law on the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In other words, resubordination does not change the status of a civilian police officer from that of a civilian to that of a military personnel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I said in my previous response that those police officers who were resubordinated, either for a short or a longer period of time, resubordinated to the army, have to carry out the orders of the military commander in line with the principle of singleness of command and subordination. However, Article 13 of the Law on Military Court is explicit, and it said that the military court has exclusive jurisdiction over military personnel. Therefore, it is the status that determines the jurisdiction. And I would like to reiterate that, in practice, this issue hasn't been clarified either at the time of the former Yugoslavia, although I can't say that we had the same situation as we had in 1992 onwards. If I remember correctly, due to the fact that this question raises a whole set of delicate issues -- for example, if an investigation is launched and is conducted by military organs, would they be allowed to interview the police officers or not? That is, for example, one of the questions. Another question which is, in my view, also a delicate one, deals with interconnectivity --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down due to the complexity of his answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, the interpreters are having a little bit of difficulty in keeping up with you. So I would ask you to bear in mind that what you say has to be interpreted and having regard to the technical nature of the answers that you are giving. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we see in this definition of military --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that this definition under Article 3 includes reserve personnel while on military duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honours. Perhaps the witness should be allowed to -- I'm sorry. I interposed with the witness. Perhaps the witness should be allowed to finish the answer to his question which wasn't recorded because he was asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, perhaps can you rephrase the question that -- where the witness was interrupted and asked to -- where the interpreters refer to the complexity of his answer. The -- because as you would note from the transcript, the -- the answer that is recorded is incomplete. I think that is the point that Mr. Zecevic is making.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me then just reiterate my previous question which was: Under this law under Article 3, this tells us, as you've testified, under this definition, subordinated police officer, resubordinated police officers would not be military personnel. And my question was: That resubordination does not change the legal status of police officers from that of civilians to that of military personnel. And part of your answer got cut off.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: In my understanding, they do not change their status. The provisions of Article 13 of the Law on Military Court, is the military courts who have exclusive jurisdiction over military personnel who have committed criminal offence. If it happens that both a member of the military and a civilian policeman commit a crime as accomplices, regardless of the policeman's state being a civilian one, then the jurisdiction would be with the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we see under this Article 3 definition that it includes reserve personnel while on military duty. So until a reservist begins performing his military duties, he was considered a civilian for purposes of criminal jurisdiction; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you could take now a look at Article 9, which is on the same page for you, Mr. Jovicinac; but if we can turn to page 2 of the English. We see that this provision permits the army to be replenished by volunteers which are defined as persons joining the army at their own request without war-time assignment. Who would fall under this definition?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: This definition encompasses only those individuals who have no war assignment but they expressed a desire to make their contribution to combat. Such individuals are requested to report with units, they are registered, and upon arrival at the unit, they become members of the military and are entitled to enjoy all the rights and benefits, as prescribed by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So this article would not apply to resubordinated police officers?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I now want to look at chapter 7, which is page 8 in your copy of the document; page 9 in the English version. And I want to focus your attention to section 2 which is disciplinary liability. And can you confirm that these were the disciplinary provisions that applied to the military in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you can look at Article 63, it states: "Military personnel who, during their service or in connection with their service, violate military discipline in an act of premeditation or negligence, shall be responsible for a breach of discipline or disciplinary offence." So by its terms, these disciplinary provisions only apply to members of the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: These disciplinary provisions did not apply to members of the civilian police who were resubordinated temporarily to the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Correct. They were not applied to police officers. Disciplinary responsibility of policemen is governed by the Law on Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have on the screen P1284.7. Mr. Jovicinac, this is tab 1; and this is, again, the Law on Military Courts that you reviewed with Judge Harhoff. And I would like you to first take a look at Article 9 under this law. And Article 9 which is page 2, I believe, both the B/C/S and the English version. This article defines who is military personnel or a military serviceman for purposes of the military courts' jurisdiction. And if you can look at items number 1 through 4 of the first paragraph, these essentially contain the same definition as we found in Article 3 of the Law on the Military; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, item number 5 includes: "A civilian performing specific military duties." Can you tell us to whom that relates?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: This relates to civilians performing certain duties connected with the defence. They work at the Ministry of Defence and are involved in mobilisation and -- this is what this refers to. So if a civilian is carrying out a military duty, then this provision pertains to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That provision would not apply to a civilian police officer resubordinated to the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, it would not apply; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question was I just wanted to verify your last answer. This item number 5, that would not include civilian police officers resubordinated to the military?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. As I see it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the second paragraph under this Article 9, it states a civilian within the meaning of this law shall be considered a person who, under the first paragraph, is not a serviceman or a prisoner of war. So a civilian police officer resubordinated to the military would fall under this catch-all definition of a civilian; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: First of all, a police officer is not a civilian. He has a status of a policeman. They have uniforms. They have weapons. They have their authority. Therefore, they cannot be considered civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I understand that, sir. But will you agree that for purposes of this law, they would be -- they would fall under the category of civilians because they're neither a member of the military, nor are they prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, then I'm going to have to ask you to clarify that because as you were testifying previously, when Judge Harhoff was asking you questions, you stated that if a police officer, I believe, committed a crime under Article 13, they would be classified as a civilian and they would be prosecuted by the military court based upon that. Now you're telling us that they do not fall under the definition or the definition of civilian for purposes of this particular law. And so could you please clarify.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Please, a policeman can, in no way, be a civilian. If he commits a crime in complicity with a member of the military, he would be processed by the military court as a policeman, not as a civilian. He is an official, and you cannot define an official in that way. Now, this could lead us into a wide debate about how the law defines the term "civilian." It does not relate to policemen, but, rather, to individuals who perform certain duties for the defence system.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on and maybe we can clarify this issue as we go along. If you can look at Article 13. And you went over this with Judge Harhoff so I won't go over it completely with you at this point, but the first paragraph deals with instances where civilians commit particular crimes under the SFRY Criminal Code. Will you agree that if a civilian police officer committed one of these crimes that under this first paragraph, the military court would have jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If the offence comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the military court and the police officer has committed such an offence, to my mind, he would be tried by a military court. Because, otherwise -- otherwise I don't know how it could be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, after the first paragraph, we have three additional paragraphs under Article 13 dealing with other instances in which the military court had jurisdiction over persons who did not fall within the definition of a military personnel. And if we can look at the second paragraph, this concerns civilians committing property and misconduct crimes against military equipment or weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So, in this instance, under this paragraph, the crimes are not limited to those enumerated in the first paragraph, under the SFRY Criminal Code?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And perhaps it is obvious from the provision itself. But unlike the first paragraph, this paragraph is not limited to certain provisions in the SFRY Criminal Code, so it could also include crimes that were perhaps covered by the Criminal Codes within the independent --or the individual republics?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. And provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can look at the third paragraph, this paragraph concerns civilians employed by the armed forces. So who would that cover, civilians employed by the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Those were civilians serving in the armed forces. Furthermore, persons in the staffs of the Territorial Defence while they are carrying out military exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That would not include civilian police officers, whether or not they had been resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, finally, in the fourth paragraph, this gives military courts jurisdiction over prisoners of war for any ordinary crimes that they may commit, as well as international war crimes; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And by way of an example, if we can turn to P2377. This is under tab 5 [sic] of your binder.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: 5 to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is tab 25. P2377. This is a decision by the deputy military prosecutor for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, dated 14 February 1993. And we see in the first paragraph that the deputy prosecutor states that the military has no subject matter jurisdiction against this accused for the crime under Article 144 of the SFRY Criminal Code, war crime against prisoners of war. Then in the third paragraph, he gives his reasons. The prosecutor explains that this case concerns a civilian person over whom the jurisdiction of the military court is not provided for under the Law of the Military Courts, Article 13. So, Mr. Jovicinac, here is a decision that is applying Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to return now to P1284.7. This is the Law on the Military Courts. And I want us to look at Article 15, which is on page 3. And we can see that Article 15 concerns the situation where a civilian and a member of the military co-perpetrated a crime. Can you tell us what was the effect of this provision?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: This provision had the following effect: It obliges the military court to try perpetrators of crimes because a member of the military was a co-perpetrator. It follows from Article 13 that the military court had exclusive jurisdiction over trying members of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at this first paragraph under Article 15. It states: "If a serviceman and a civilian, exclusive of persons under Article 13, paragraph 4, which is relating to POWs, had committed a crime as accomplices, and if the trial of the civilian falls within the jurisdiction of another regular court, this court will also try the serviceman." Doesn't this paragraph have the effect of giving the civilian courts jurisdiction over crimes committed or co-perpetrated by members of the military?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I don't think this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please interpret that paragraph then for us. What do they mean by regular courts would have jurisdiction over the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Another regular court would be -- in plain language would be the civilian court that has jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So as I read this provision in this plain language, the civilian court would have jurisdiction in this instance?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. Do read the last sentence here. It says in this paragraph that: "This court will also try the serviceman." That means the serviceman and the civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: It I'm referring to paragraph 3 of Article 15, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you are saying when they refer to "this court," they're not referring to the regular court, but they're referring to the military court, under your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. No. Please. We should read the entire paragraph. As an exception to paragraph 1 of this article, if a serviceman has committed a crime of official misconduct and a civilian appears as a co-perpetrator or an accomplice, a military court will try both the serviceman and the civilian, if we are referring to paragraph 2. If we read paragraph 3, then we see the following: "If in connection with the commitment of a crime by servicemen or by a person under Article 13 of this law and a civilian, and if one of them has aided or abetted the perpetrator after the commission of the crime, or if he did not report the preparation of the crime, the commission of the crime or the perpetrator, the trial shall fall within the jurisdiction of the court having jurisdiction over the perpetrator."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, I'm interested -- I'm sorry. I'm interested in paragraph 1, not the second or third paragraph. The first paragraph. And this -- that paragraph, the first paragraph --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- states that where you have a serviceman and a civilian, and the civilian would ordinarily fall under the regular courts, the regular court will also try the military serviceman; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. In such a case, the military court has exclusive jurisdiction. We read that in the last line of paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would ask you to look at -- well, let me just read this to you. This is from your interview --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, excuse me. No, no. It was my mistake. If a serviceman and a civilian, exclusive of persons under Article 13, paragraph 4 of this law, committed a crime as an accomplices or co-perpetrators and if the trial of the civilian falls within the jurisdiction of another regular court, this court will also try the serviceman. So, in such a case, the serviceman will be then held responsible before a regular court rather than a military court. I apologise. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No problem. I just wanted to make sure we were clear on that. Now, if we could turn to Article 16, can you confirm that I interpreted this provision correctly. This Article 16 addresses a situation where a member of the military commits a crime but then leaves the army before he is indicted by the military court. Can you tell us what the effect of this provision was?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If it's a criminal offence that falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of military courts, then he will be tried by a military court. If not, and the indictment has not legal force yet, then he will be tried by a regular court, that is, a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I just want to return to Article 15 one last time. If we can have 65 ter 2069 on the screen. This is the document that Judge Harhoff had shown you. And we can see from the first paragraph that the perpetrators are suspected of committing murder under Article 36 of the BiH Criminal Code. In your answer to Judge Harhoff, you mention that if one of these perpetrators was determined to be a civilian, that the case would be heard by the military court. Now we've looked at Article 15 which deals with co-perpetrators where there's servicemen and civilians co-perpetrating a crime. Under the -- Article 15, in fact, this case, if it involved both civilian and military persons, would fall under the civilian court's jurisdiction, under Article 15 of the Law on Military Courts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. For this offence, since these persons are members of the military and they can be tried exclusively by a military court, we're not talking about aiding and abetting or anything. We are talking about perpetrators. Although the information isn't complete, it still follows from the preamble, that is, the first paragraph, that they are military conscripts, members of the 6th Krajina Brigade, which means that they are members of the military. And they are suspected of having committed the crime of murder under Article 36, and so on. So that the military court has jurisdiction even if, amongst them, there was a civilian or a police officer because under Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts, it is clearly stipulated that the -- that a military court has exclusive jurisdiction over crimes committed by members of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, we understand that. But we were talking about Article 15 of that law, which deals with co-perpetration. And in those instances, if it is an ordinary crime that doesn't fall under Article 13, the civilian court has jurisdiction over it. We could look back at Article 15 which is P1284.7, tab 1. Sir, do you need me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I understand your question. Article 13, military courts try civilians for the following criminal offences contained in the Criminal Code of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But I want to focus your attention on Article 15, which deals with the issue of co-perpetration. And I want to understand: Does this article apply to the case we look -- just looked at, if the crime of murder was committed by both military personnel, as well as civilian persons?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: There are no civilians here. It follows from the preamble that they are all members of the 6th Krajina Brigade, military conscripts. But I said a civilian would be tried by a military if one had been amongst them because an offence, and that falls under Article 36, is in the exclusive jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to spend much more time on this, but Article 36 is referring to the BiH Criminal Code and that does not fall under Article 13; isn't that correct? Article 13 outlines the provisions of the SFRY Criminal Code. Article 36 is from the BiH Criminal Code. And it's ordinary murder.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is qualified murder. In this case, since the co-perpetrators were members of the military and civilians, if a civilian court had jurisdiction over these matters, then the members of the military would also be tried by the court that has jurisdiction. Although there's no logic in that, but what can you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk -- we've spoken about the Article 16 and its effect on a member of the military who commits a crime and then leaves the military service. I want to talk about the reverse situation. If a civilian police officer commits a crime but then is transferred to the army, not resubordinated but transferred to the army, did the civilian courts maintain jurisdiction over that old crime that was committed by the police officer when he was a civilian?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: A member of the military is tried by a military court for the offences that he committed when he was a member of the military. He couldn't be tried for such offences by a military court, though, but by a civilian court where the proceedings were instigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I now want to discuss with you the procedural process of becoming a member of the military. Can you tell us: For a member of the police to become a member of the military, what had to happen? What kind of process had to happen?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Under the laws and regulations in force, that person had to be discharged from his service, and that's under the Law on Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object to this line of questioning. I object to this line of questioning by the Prosecutor because this goes beyond the matters that the Trial Chamber dealt with. We're talking about courts' jurisdiction and possibility the integrity of this witness. But this is clearly beyond the scope of these -- of this subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, perhaps it is necessary for you to narrow your question to conform to the purposes limited -- limited purposes for which this witness was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps I could explain why I'm asking this question. We've established now through this witness that the military courts prosecutor's office had jurisdiction over military personnel and now I'm exploring at what point would a police officer become military personnel. What kind of -- I need to establish what the process is, and then I can ask the witness at what point would that police officer become military personnel for purposes of the Law on the Army and the Law on Military Courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, I take it you understand what Mr. Olmsted has just explained. So within that narrow compass, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, the police officer had to be discharged from the force, then he must be registered as a military conscript by the draft office, and then sent to serve with a military unit. On the day when he reports to that unit, he, effectively, becomes a member of the military. That would be it, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And it is at that point in time that if he committed a crime that the military courts would exercise jurisdiction over him?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to me whether you're referring to a point in time before that person has reported to the unit or after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm referring to the point where they reported to the unit. At that point in time, when they've shown up to the unit to carry on military duties, that is when the military courts and prosecutor's offices had jurisdiction over that individual; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You've mentioned that once a person joins the military, that's registered somewhere. Can you confirm that that would be registered in the Vob 8 form, as well as that individual's military booklet?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these documents, the Vob 8 form, as well as the military booklet, were the documents that the military police - and, if necessary, the military's prosecutor's office - would consult to determine whether they had jurisdiction over that individual; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. If there is any suspicion or if any need arises for conducting a check, whether this individual is, indeed, a member of the military or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we take a look at tab 8 of your binder. This is 65 ter 30001. Mr. Jovicinac, could you confirm with us this is what a Vob 8 register looked like back in 1992? And perhaps we can turn to page 3 --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what level in the military hierarchy this register was maintained?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Each basic unit maintained such records. And I mean by that an independent battalion, regiment, and brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And for each unit, this register would record all military personnel for that unit, from the commander, all the way to the last soldier, and included reserve soldiers as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: A civilian police officer who was resubordinated to the military would not appear in this register; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't, at least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence. It's not only relevant to the issue of determining a status of a person but also it's relevant to a pending rebuttal motion that the Prosecution has filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we object because the pending rebuttal motion deals with ABiH Vob forms and this has nothing to do with the -- with the -- with the JNA or VRS Vob forms. And this is not relevant at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I find it strange that you would anticipate a document becoming relevant by the determination on a motion that has yet to be decided upon, so I would disregard that arm of your argument. But in terms of this document itself, having regard to this witness's testimony, isn't the evidence that the -- what we are concerned about, that this is -- this establishes the negative? So how is this relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct, Your Honour. It does establish the negative. However, the Prosecution feels that it would be good to have an example of one of these registers on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For what purpose? We have -- you showed it to the witness. The witness has given an answer. I see no utility at all to this document as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will show that there are no police officers listed in this register. And, therefore, it corroborates what the witness has been saying: That civilian police resubordinated would not appear in this particular register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, if you were to prove that there were no policemen registered by way of the Vob 8 formulas, then you would have to show us all the Vob 8 formulas that would apply to the entire VRS and then show to us that in none of these any policeman was registered. But showing us one example wouldn't make the point. I think we have the witness's testimony and that would suffice, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, point taken. I'll retract the motion to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can please look at P2344. This is tab 3, Mr. Jovicinac, in your binder. And, sir, can you confirm that this is an example of a military booklet, how it existed back in 1992.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you can please turn to page 7 of your copy, and page 15 of the English.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we can go back two pages in the English version. I see the page numbers at the bottom don't correspond with the pages in e-court. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, according to this military booklet, this person's war-time assignment was with the RS Ministry of Interior from the 4th of April, 1992, until the 30th of June, 1996. Based upon this booklet, Mr. Jovicinac, if this person was arrested during this period for committing a crime which did not fall under Article 13, the military authorities would have turned this person over to the civilian authorities - isn't that correct? - because, according to this booklet, he was a member of the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Look, if we are talking about perpetrators and their arrests, if the military police or any other member of the military caught someone in flagrante, they would have been obliged to report this to the nearest police station so that they would come over and take over this individual, and there is reciprocity in that as well. If the police caught a military personnel committing a crime, it is their duty to call the military police to come over and arrest the perpetrator for further interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Until a perpetrator of a crime was identified as a member of the military, the civilian authorities maintained jurisdiction over that case; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So if an unknown perpetrator case was brought to you, you would send it to the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: If it is not within the exclusive jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 1358 on the screen. This is tab 16. And we can see this is a report on crime trends for September 1992 from the 1st Krajina Corps military prosecutor's office. Can you confirm for us that this is one of your office's reports for the month of September 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would like you to turn to page 19 in your version, and we could turn to page 20 in the English.
