The first paragraph, under Roman numeral IV, preventative activities, states that the military prosecutor's office consulted with the civilian courts, prosecutor's offices, Security Services Centres on the demarcation of jurisdiction. Do you see that in the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: To your knowledge, in the course of these consultations, did the issue of jurisdiction over crimes committed by the civilian police ever come up?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I did not personally take part in this. This was this initial period that I mentioned before, but I think that if you arrive at certain conclusions, I think that something is missing here. Although, in spite of that, I wouldn't be able to give you a more precise answer than this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the third paragraph then. It states that seminars were held on the subject of disciplinary responsibility of military personnel with the most responsible officers of the 2nd Krajina Corps, air force, PVO, and with secretaries, judges and military disciplinary prosecutors. So can you confirm that the military prosecutor's office, as part of its responsibilities, provided training on military disciplinary responsibility?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Look, this is what we call general prevention. These seminars were organised by units. According to what I know, the military prosecutor's office offered professional assistance. These seminars were even used at an opportunity to train the people collecting evidence about the perpetrators of crimes, about the detection of crimes, and that it was a useful exercise that the commands, in co-operation with the military prosecutor office, conducted. After such seminars, criminal reports became much better. They contained more information and more compelling evidence which facilitated the whole process of prosecution. Now, let me go back to chapter 6. No, this is chapter 4. Where were we a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. We were looking at chapter Roman numeral IV.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, chapter IV. Chapter IV. I can't speak about the intricacies, but I suppose that the then-prosecutor thought it appropriate to maintain contacts with civilian prosecutors, as well as representatives of the MUP so that, in a way, work and co-operation can be improved. And I'm talking about co-ordination between military and civilian organ, specifically military police, military security, civilian's police and civilian security services, because there are some provisions that are common for all these entities in the Law on Criminal Procedure. As for the rest of it, I cannot give you any more of my opinion because I wasn't involved in this. But, nonetheless, I thought this was a useful approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, is this a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: When we resume, you would have 22 minutes left. Mr. Jovicinac, we are about to take our second break. We will resume in another 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know why I was waiting for the witness to be escorted inside. Mr. Jovicinac, we are back, and Mr. Olmsted is about to wind up his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Before you begin ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In terms of the -- thank you. In terms of the time left with this witness, when Mr. Olmsted would have completed his cross-examination -- and, Mr. Witness, we have already alerted you that we may -- that we would take a break at 1.45 and continue for some time after that, so the -- we would -- when Mr. Olmsted has completed his -- his cross-examination, we would then move to the Defence, and we would then take a break at 1.45 at which time, and I say this for those of us here, we would reconvene in Courtroom II, at -- in an hour? At 2.45. Yes. Thank you. Please, continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 1358 back on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is tab 16, Mr. Jovicinac, in your binder. And if we can turn back to page 19 in your version; page 20 of the English version. Sir, before the break, I was asking you some questions with regard to paragraph 3 under this preventative activities section of this document. And paragraph 3 raises the issue of disciplinary measures and seminars and other consultations that the military prosecutor's office had on this particular issue. My question for is: To your knowledge, did the issue of disciplinary measures against police officers resubordinated to the military ever come up in any of these discussions or consultations or seminars?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I attended some of these seminars, but there was no discussion about initiating disciplinary procedures against members of the police, for the simple reason that the police have their own rules governing disciplinary responsibilities and the measures prescribed as sanctions which are somewhat different from the measures and proceedings conducted by military disciplinary court. They are different from the police disciplinary courts. So, as far as I can remember, this issue was not debated, nor ever tackled at all. These seminars were organised by the commands, and the prosecutor's office only rendered professional help. As far as I can remember, even some of the judges took part in those seminars in order to offer their professional help, because the majority of the units was made up of reservists which was not exactly -- category who were well versed in rules and regulations. All of this was done with a view to strengthening the discipline and enhancing the military organisation, in order to make it able of carrying out the tasks that it had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: One of the reasons that subordinated or resubordinated police units were commanded by a senior member of the police was for this very reason, to address any disciplinary measures against the police; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. Please. There is a by-law in the army which regulates military discipline. It prescribes in very detailed terms the disciplinary measures that can be imposed on members of the military for disciplinary offences. Let me be more clear. Disciplinary measures can be pronounced either directly by a direct superior officer in line with his powers, and for disciplinary violations, proceedings have to be instituted, which is followed by an indictment, because there is also a military disciplinary prosecutor who presents his case before the military disciplinary panel made up of three judges and a registrar who is a professional organ, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: -- this is described in great detail in the rules governing the military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. What I was after was not a description of the military disciplinary procedures. Unfortunately, we don't have time to go into those details. My question was fairly simple: A resubordinated police unit had a senior police commander at the head of that unit; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that question because I am not familiar with the chain of command in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. This document also mentions that Kamenica and Manjaca prisoner of war camps were visited. These were the two VRS POW camps under the 1st Krajina Corps' jurisdiction in 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were there any others?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than these two POW camps, were you aware of any other that were -- fell under the 1st Krajina Corps' jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you visit either of these camps in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: When you were asked about Manjaca camp back during your 2002 interview, you stated you that you had no information about Manjaca camp, it was not in your jurisdiction, and you were never consulted about it. Do you maintain that position today?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 1D411 on the screen. This is tab 17, Mr. Jovicinac, in your binder. Mr. Jovicinac, this is a letter from the 1st Krajina Corps Command, General Talic, to CSB Banja Luka and the 43rd Motorised Brigade of the 1st Krajina Corps, dated the 16th of October, 1992. And General Talic is forwarding a telegram he received from the VRS Main Staff informing them that Prijedor police unit members have abandoned their positions and fled back to their towns. This was a pretty significant event in 1992 in which a large number of soldiers and police officers abandoned the front lines in Han Pijesak. Do you recall this incident?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that because that was not within the area of responsibility or within the area of jurisdiction of Banja Luka. Han Pijesak lies within the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor's office in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This telegram is sent to the CSB Banja Luka. Was that because the civilian police had responsibility to investigate this matter, at least to the extent it applied to civilian police officers?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: That is something that undoubtedly arises from this telegram, because they are their superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If -- if the crime that is determined that they committed in the end was that of desertion under Article 217 of the SFRY Criminal Code, then the CSB should file the criminal reports with the military prosecutor's office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, we are going back to when I said that this was a very delicate or sensitive issue. It may amount to this crime alone. However, if you look at the nature of the crime and those who may be its perpetrators, as well as the decision governing military courts, the question arises as to whether, based on the legal provisions in place, the police can be held answerable under that law. If they cannot held responsible, then such a crime does not exist. It would be logical for that responsibility to exist. However, truth to tell, this is the first time I'm seeing this and I'm hearing of this. The military prosecutor's office had never received a case such as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Than was my next question. You were not aware of receiving any criminal reports with regard to this incident?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Please. Excuse me. There is something I didn't pay attention to over here, if I am allowed to proceed? Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Annexed here is a list of military conscripts; that's to say, reserve policemen who had abandoned their positions. In my understanding, this would have had to be prosecuted before a military court. It reads, "A list of conscripts, reserve policemen." This is the crucial line that can lean towards either side but it is a -- an offence that comes under Article 217. That is without doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But it's clear that Talic, General Talic is seeking the CSB to take action against these police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object to that. Where is that? Can you quote it? Where is this? He asked CSB for that, or is it your misinterpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, my question, and I will repeat it because I believe I'm entitled to ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Is that General Talic is expecting the CSB to take some action with regard to these police officers; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's calling for speculation. Where is that in this letter? Can you quote it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Cvijetic, could you assist -- I'm not sure I follow your objection because the document on its face would seem to bear no other logical meaning than the proposition that is being put by Mr. Olmsted. What am I missing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: After all, it is address -- it is from General Talic, addressed to CSB Banja Luka. So what -- what am I not getting?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the Defence get into this, I think it's better that the witness not participate in this discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jovicinac, could you remove your headphones for a second, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were not able to understand my objection because I haven't made one. Your Honours, the document clearly indicates that the Main Staff orders the command of the 1st Krajina Corps to issue criminal reports against the perpetrators of this crime. We discussed this issue with a previous witness and pointed to these quotation marks, because this is a quote from a letter sent by the Main Staff. So the Main Staff orders the command of the 1st Krajina Corps to file criminal charges against individuals, that names be published, et cetera. Now, the command of the 1st Krajina Corps proceeds only to send this for information to the CSB and the 43rd Mechanised Brigade, or what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that's the position of the Defence and that's the position that was taken by the Defence expert who, of course, never saw this document either. But that is not the position of the Prosecution. And as Your Honour has pointed out, it can be open to that interpretation, and I'm -- the Prosecution's position on its interpretation and that's what I'm exploring with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- it seems to me that you can explore that -- the question as phrased is unobjectionable. The -- could the Court Officer have the witness replace his headphones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise for that, Mr. Jovicinac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Olmsted, would you bear in mind, having regard to what Mr. Cvijetic explains and as you reminded us about the position that they have taken, that the document is capable of other meaning. So you would -- the -- those nuances should be apparent in the question that you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, as you testified earlier, it is clear that General Talic is sending this telegram he received from the VRS Main Staff to the CSB because he expected the CSB to take some actions on this; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, you would agree that it would be standard practice for General Talic to involve the MUP in any criminal investigation involving civilian police officers.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. You said that I testified about it earlier, and I don't recall testifying on this issue at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. But my question is: You would agree that it would be standard practice for General Talic to involve the MUP in any criminal investigation of civilian police officers. That would be normal, under the principle of reciprocity that you described earlier.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. In situations such as this one, General Talic would -- well, now that I looked at page 2 of this document, there is a list of soldiers who left their positions between 13 September and 19 October, 71 of them, without a list of civilian policemen. So this was a mixed group abandoning positions. Under those circumstances, if there were civilian policemen among them who deserted their positions, as well as the army, as well as soldiers, then it was only natural that the MUP should be informed about it and that co-ordinated measures should be taken as envisaged under the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, of course, the police hierarchy, the MUP, would still maintain disciplinary authority over any of these 71 individuals who happened to be members of the police.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I disassociated myself from such a statement. I distance myself from it. If you look at page 2 of this telegram, the list appended, it says the list of soldier who abandoned positions, who went AWOL. Is this an error or not? That I don't know. But the annex says the list of conscripts, reserve policemen. So there must be a link in between that is missing here. Based on this list, I don't know if they are policemen or soldiers. It says here, undoubtedly, quite clearly that these were soldiers who abandoned their positions. If they were soldiers, then they fell within the sole jurisdiction of the military justice administration, and it was the security organs or the military policemen who were duty-bound to gather all the relevant information and evidence to compile a criminal report and send it to the prosecutor's -- military prosecutor's office with jurisdiction. Evidently, there were policemen among them who abandoned positions too, and since this act was committed simultaneously, they were supposed to be criminally investigated by the MUP. And since they perpetrated this crime together with soldiers, it would have been within the jurisdiction of a military court to prosecute this case further, if this unit was resubordinated to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to go back to my original question. The MUP would still, no matter what, maintain disciplinary authority over these police officers, if this list, in fact, includes civilian police officers?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think we can perhaps clarify this issue of who is on this list, Your Honours, if I show this witness a couple of documents that we uncovered in preparation for this witness's testimony. And if I can have leave to do that. I would like to show -- first of all, I would like to have the witness take note.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, can you please turn to page 3 of your document with the list of 71 names, and if you could just take notes of the names under entries 2 --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If you please take a look at the names under entries 2, 4, 6, 7, 11, 12, 15, 16 and 18. And now if you could take a look at tab 19. This is 65 ter 30004. And, sir, this is a list of military conscripts in the Military Police Company securing the city and it's signed by military police commander in Prijedor and it is dated the 30th of October, 1992, so around the time of the document that we just looked at. And if you look under entries 12 to 14, 16, 18, 19, 21 and 23, those are, in fact, the names that we looked at in the previous document.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So those individuals were members of the military. They were members of the military police, in fact?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, if can you please go back to tab 17 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, your time has expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And that's why I sought leave of this Trial Chamber just to explore this confusion over who is on this list. I just have this last document to show him, and then I'm through. Your Honours, I wonder if we should tender that last document into evidence, however, because it does contain the names of certain individuals on this 1D411 and therefore provides some clarity to the issue of who these 71 individuals were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I do object. Because whatever Mr. Olmsted is trying to establish here, he is not establishing that because we cannot possibly identify by the names persons on two lists. First of all, this witness does not know anything about it. The second thing is there might be at least two -- two persons with the same name, so we don't know whether this is the -- this one list refers to another individual or the first list to another individual. Therefore, I don't really see the -- the point of -- of admitting this document, because it is inconclusive evidence all together. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that goes to weight and, of course, argument. With regard to whether they're the same individuals, we would submit that they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But on what basis? Taken at its highest, is it possible to, just by comparing the two documents, arrive at the conclusion that you would invite us to arrive at?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the documents are close in time. They both involve Prijedor, and the entries I just went through, there are nine. So at least nine names are similar on the two lists. And, therefore, we would submit -- and the military police platoon in Prijedor would have been under the 43rd Motorised Brigade. So we would say that that evidence collectively would establish that these are the same people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the previous document is admitted and marked, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, if we can please look at tab 17 again --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2453, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, if you can look again at tab 17, again at the list of 71 names. And please take note of these particular names on that document: Entries 29, Mladen Timarac; 30, Nenad Ecim; 34, Radenko Lukic; 44, Dragan Jeftic; 66, Branko Knezevic; and, 67, Lazar Matijis. And now if you can turn to tab 26 in your binder. This is it 65 ter 30007. What we have is a list of special police unit members under the command of Miroslav Paras, who are sent to the Orasje front and it's signed by the SJB Prijedor chief, Simo Drljaca, and it's dated the 25th of February, 1993. And if you look at the names I just mentioned, if you look under 4, 5, 12, 13, 14 and 16, those individuals from the previous list were, in fact, members of SJB Prijedor; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know if they were members or not. In my view, the lists are incomplete because they should contain full name, first and family name, and father's name. The fact of the matter is that these individuals can be found on both these lists and that goes to show that these individuals abandoned their positions with those other members of that military police company. That is my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to confirm, you have no recollection of any criminal reports filed against these members of SJB Prijedor for abandoning their position. You don't recall receiving any criminal reports?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Neither from the military nor the civilian police. No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would like to tender this document for the same reason as it provides clarity to the exhibit 1D411.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2454, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that concludes my questions. I forgot to seek to tender the document I showed the witness before and immediately after the break which was 65 ter 1358, the report from the military prosecutor's office from September 1992 that we talked about at some length. I would move to admit that into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We had noted that you hadn't so moved and we thought you had wisely chosen not to tender it because it adds nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we would disagree as it establishes that the military prosecutor and military courts were involved in addressing issues of disciplinary -- discipline of military personnel, and -- in 1992, as well as visited the POW camps, as well as discussed jurisdictional issues with civilian and military authorities. And so in that way it corroborates what this witness has been saying about what he understood were the issues back in 1992 with regard to jurisdiction, disciplinary matters, and such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But that's all a part of the record, isn't it, Mr. Olmsted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But the document itself is further evidence of that and it corroborates the witness. Obviously this witness -- this document has been in the hands of the Defence for many years now, three or four years, and therefore, there's no prejudice to the Defence and the Prosecution would seek to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may our objection be recorded as well. It's not the point whether this document has been in possession of the -- of the Defence so how many years or something. The point of the matter is at which stage of the proceedings the trial -- the Office of the Prosecutor is trying to tender it. And what is the actual relevance of this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours I could not -- I didn't have time to explore the entire document with this witness, but the witness did authenticate it as a report from his office, and, therefore, we would tender it in for other purposes for what the document states. But in particular for this witness, I explained the relevance for -- with regard to his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is not persuaded the document should be admitted. I assume that Defence counsel have -- has decided how to divide up their work and the time. So, Mr. Krgovic, I see you on your feet. I infer from that that you are beginning. And I would remind you that you have 90 minutes to share between you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello, Mr. Jovicinac.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that we can barely hear Mr. Krgovic. He needs to come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Mr. Jovicinac?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, I will follow up on the last answer you gave to my learned friend, Mr. Olmsted, when you said that you had no occasion to see any of such criminal reports, either filed by the civilian police or military police in relation to this event. And the reason for that is that, since this had happened in Han Pijesak, this incident did not fall under the jurisdiction of your prosecutor's office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the answers you gave to the Prosecutor, and also based on the interview you gave previously, in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps covered by your prosecutor's office at the time when you started working, expect for Jajce, there were no other combat activities in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, as a result, you, through your daily work, had no occasion to come across this phenomenon of resubordination of the military -- of the police to the military in combat activities because at the time it simply didn't come across your daily activities. It didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Consequently, the answers given by you to the Prosecutor and the Chamber were based on your logic and on your previous experience, and also it was based on the documents shown to you by the Chamber and the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The answers you gave did not stem from a particular specific case that you dealt with in your career, or they did not come as a result of your participation in some legal work-shop or seminar where such topics were discussed; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I said was that the answers you gave -- perhaps my question was simply too long. You're right. But the answers that you gave to the Prosecutor and the Chamber did not come as a result of you personally dealing with a case, with a relevant case, or did not come as a result of your participation in the legal seminar where such topics were discussed. You simply answered based on logic; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, let us now go back to what the Prosecutor explored in the beginning of his examination, the notion of a conscript which is mentioned in a number of documents in the law and is also something that you came across in your practice. You will agree with me that policemen also constitute military conscripts. They also fall in that category of conscripts; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Those policemen who are mobilised for combat, they also fall under the category of military conscript; whereas, other policemen, who are not mobilised, do not fall into that category.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the reserve policemen do come under the category of military conscripts; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krgovic. How is it that from the answer to the previous question you're able to conclude that reserve policemen do come under the category of military conscripts? Something I'm missing there, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's a mistake in interpretation. My question was: Reserve policemen fall in the category of military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, can you please repeat your answer to my question whether policemen are also military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: A policeman is a military conscript as long as his name is in the military records in the Ministry of Defence. Following --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Witness. Witness. The interpreters ask you to repeat the question, please -- to repeat the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness needs to speak slower because the sound is blurred and we cannot tell whether he says mobilisation or demobilisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All individuals who are in reserve forces and who are in the military records of the Secretariat for National Defence are considered as military conscripts. Once the mobilisation is carried out, those who are mobilised for the purposes of the military go into military units. They become military personnel with the same rights and duties as all other military personnel. As for military conscripts who were mobilised, or whose war-time assignment is in the police, they acquire the status of a policeman, and they have the same rights and obligations as other policemen. A military conscript for as long as he is in the military records of the Secretariat of the National Defence are considered as military personnel. Secretariat does not mobilise only for the purposes of the military or police. Secretariat also mobilises people for civilian defence and all other structures, and all military conscripts who are assigned to those structures fall under the rules and regulations that exist for those structures. I hope I was able to clarify this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, I would remind you that the interpreters have to keep up with you, so please slow down when answering the questions, sir. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the times of immediate threat of war, for somebody to become a military conscript that person does not need to be in the military records. At military conscript is a person who is fit for military service in the time of an imminent threat of war. Therefore, that person does not even need to be in the military records with the Secretariat of National Defence. He needs -- he will have automatically the status of a military conscripts if it is in the immediate -- period of the immediate threat of war?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I do not agree with you. Anybody who is fit for military service, according to the Law on National Defence, is recorded in the records of the Secretariat for National Defence. And the secretariat, at the request of military units or police, assigns such persons, issues call-up papers and gives them their assignment. This is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you that you are not right and that what I said is the position taken by the supreme military prosecutor's office, and I will put documents to you showing this. I'm also putting to you that given that you do not have any practical experience -- or, rather, you did not have experience with such cases back in 1992, you, as a result of that, did not give me the correct answer. Further on, Mr. Jovicinac, a policeman, once he is resubordinated and once he takes part in combat activities, is carrying out a military duty; right? He is discharging a military duty.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: In my answer, I said that this does have the characteristics of a military duty. However, when it comes to the jurisdiction of military courts that revolves around the status, neither the case law nor the theory, legal theory, ever dealt with this issue, even though what these persons are doing has all the hallmarks of a military duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you will agree with me that when a policeman takes part in combat activities and when he is attacked by an enemy soldier and killed, he is considered a legitimate target. He can fire, he can attack, and the opposing side can treat him as a legitimate target without being responsible for injuring somebody in the line of his official duties. This is considered combat; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's absolutely right. Not only as a policeman but also as a member of the military. He uses weapons in accordance with the rules on the use of weapons within that military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when he is resubordinated to a military command, he has the same rights and duties as all other soldiers of the unit, of his unit; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what rights and duties you're referring to, but I am concerned that due to insufficient knowledge of that topic I could give you a wrong answer. What I know and what I was able to understand, such resubordinations do not fall under my jurisdiction. That is considered command and control and the use of units. And these are the topics that should best be directed by -- to somebody who deals with command and control and the command tactics. I understood it that I was supposed to testify about the jurisdiction of military courts and military prosecutor's office, and I did it to the best of my abilities. Now, as to these rights and duties that you're referring to, I would rather not deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when I put this question to you, what I meant to ask was this: If a policeman taking part in combat activities is wounded, he would be entitled to the status of a war veteran and disabilities that come with that; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If such a policeman were to be killed, his family would enjoy all benefits as the families of a fallen soldier; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only in the cases where he is resubordinated and takes part in combat with the unit, also if he is acting separate from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you just mentioned a minute ago their status, whether they had the status of a military conscript, their rights and duties, and so on. Those who lead the combat would have more experience, more knowledge about this than you; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Listen, I really don't want to put either you or myself in a delicate situation. I said that the use of units and command and control is not something that a military prosecutor deals with, neither military courts deal with that. At any rate, what I know about resubordination is not sufficient. Resubordination could be put in place for a short period of time, for a long period of time. It can also involve co-ordinated action, but I simply don't know enough about these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me show you a document. Please look at my tab 19 in the Zupljanin binder, which is P421 -- 411 shown to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D411. I apologise. [In English] Tab 15.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Could the counsel please say the tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 15 in my binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You have just seen this document.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a letter from the Command of the 1st Krajina Corps entitled: "Abandonment of positions by police members, information"; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In this letter, they speak of cases when police members abandoned their positions. So this is the title of this document and this is what this document deals with; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, logically analysing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 2 -- rather, if you look at paragraph 1, Mr. Talic here quotes the document received by him from the Main Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in accordance with the title, he says here: "We are hereby informing you that the Prijedor police unit members have abandoned their positions ..." He speaks exclusively of them; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, here in the attachment, General Talic says: List of conscripts, reserve policemen. And he treats these reserve policemen as military conscripts; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that because this list which is attached to this letter as an entitled list of soldiers who had left their positions from the 13th of September until the 10th of October, 1992, well, for me, this document is simply incomplete. And it is very difficult for me here to give any solid explanation because the list was sent to the CSB Banja Luka and to the Command of the 1st Krajina Corps and the 43rd Motorised Brigade; therefore, this document is incomplete. It gives me some information, but I, as a prosecutor, would go to great lengths to verify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, Mr. Talic considered these policemen from the list to be soldiers. And they were, indeed, soldiers during the time that they were resubordinated; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I'm telling you're again putting me in a position not -- in which I'm not able to comment this document. It is contradictory. The first page contradicts the second page. And Mr. Prosecutor also showed me that in another list we saw members of the military police as well. I can only give you an answer in principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you cannot give me any answer at all because you have never encountered such an example in your work, nor did you have any contact, either theoretically or practically, with the issue of the status and the jurisdictions of military and civilian organs in the particular instance when we talk about resubordination. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I wouldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that when we speak about the status of resubordinated policemen, General Talic is more competent to explain that, and we can see from this document how he described their status; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Olmsted is on his feet. I think I anticipate [overlapping speakers] I think I anticipate what his objection is going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, well, perhaps. The term status is ambiguous. I mean, this witness is talking about status of the -- for purposes of the military court's jurisdiction. And there's ambiguity in what Mr. Krgovic means -- if status for purposes of resubordination or what have you, so I think there needs to be clarity on that issue. Plus I'm not sure that this witness is in a position to comment on General Talic's knowledge on a particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That was the observation that I was about to make. It seems that the point that -- if I understand it correctly, that you wish to make by that question is really something that should be reserved for argument, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in my opinion, whether the status of a member of any formation cannot be construed on a case by case basis. He is either a conscript - i.e., a soldier - or not a conscript. If someone is a conscript and enjoys some benefits as a result of that, that's a debatable issue. This is my response to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jovicinac, can we go back to this question. If someone enjoys the status of a military conscript and if such person performs military duties, and in the course of that commits a crime, would then the military prosecutor and the military court be competent to prosecute such a perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Provided he is a member of the military, yes. That means that if this person was mobilised for the purposes of military service and as of the day of his reporting at the unit this is when his status of a member of the military commences and consequently it is the military court that has the exclusive jurisdiction to prosecute them, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Excuse me. This is in accordance with the Law on Military Courts and I base my answers on that. And also it is in line with the provision of the Law on the Army which also defines who members of the armed forces are. I don't have the copy of this law in front of me. I can't tell you exactly which provision is that, but I think that there is even some mention of the status of military personnel in the criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: All I'm asking you -- I'm sorry to interrupt you, I am asking you if a person is a military conscript and if he performs military duties, so both criteria are satisfied, does he fall under the jurisdictions of military organs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, wasn't that question asked and answered, answered by the witness by adding another criteria?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, my LiveNote is dead; therefore, I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you repeat the answer that you gave because it hasn't been recorded.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: To your last question? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I asked you about the two criteria. If someone is, (A) a conscript, and (B) if he performs military duty according to these two criteria, would he fall under the jurisdiction of military judiciary organs, i.e., prosecutor's offices and courts?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said absolutely?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is really a confusing issue. I rose also at the same time that Judge Delvoie raised the issue. This witness has a great length, both during Judge Harhoff's evidence, the Prosecution's questions explained this, and it has been asked and answered now at least on three occasions, and at that point, I think, Your Honours, we object. I know this is not a typical objection in this Tribunal, but we object that these questions should not be continued to be asked of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, in addition to these two that I mentioned, is there any other requirement necessary? I asked you only about the category of those who are either conscripts and those who performed military duties. I'm sorry, did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I really don't know. You asked me this question at least four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see that you answered me.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: And I gave you at least four answers. And I also answered the same question to the Presiding Judge and to the Prosecutor. So if you analyse what the performance of military duties involves, I don't know what else can I add. A military duty is a broad notion, a very broad notion. A military duty is the person who serves the call-up papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to suggest to you a number of military duties so that we can check whether we think along the same lines. So a military duty is to take part in combat?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, under the command. Organised combat under the command. Because according to the Law on the Army, the command implies that it is organised on the principle of unity of command, subordination, and singleness of command. Everything beyond that scope cannot be considered a military duty. And this goes from the commander at the top up to the last private.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Guarding prisoners of war. That's another military duty under the command; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I don't know. If the camp was under the command of the army, then, of course, that's another military duty, and that's called guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Standing guard or guarding a camp where the troops are billeted in combat area.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: The guard and patrol duties is considered a military duty, even if it happens in peacetime. It is considered in the same way, no matter whether we have peacetime or war time, and there is a criminal offence of infringement of guard duty. And it is punishable by law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your answers, sir, I put it to you that once the police force is resubordinated to the army, number 1, it enjoys the status of military conscripts; number 2, it carries out military duties; and number 3, it falls under the jurisdiction of military judicial organs and not civilian ones. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a decisive answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jovicinac, when we speak about the competence to try criminal offences, I'm sure that your office used the rules that were used by the JNA and that were in force in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Article 12 of the Law on the Implementation of the Constitution of Republika Srpska stipulates that all the laws and by-laws and other enactments of the former SFRY and the former BH shall be implemented, pending the adoption of the Law of Republika Srpska. Among other things, we applied the rules of engagement, the Law on Military Courts, the Law on Military Prosecutor Offices, and so on and so forth. The Criminal Code of the SFRY was amongst them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit L12. That's tab 3 in the Zupljanin binder. Although, Your Honour, I think this is time for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was just going to suggest that because this is going -- probably take a little time, and we must vacate this courtroom for -- to be prepared for the trial to come up. Mr. Jovicinac, we're about to take the break, as we indicated. We will resume in an hour. You will be escorted, conducted back to the offices in Belgrade, but we will take a break, and Mr. Krgovic will continue when we resume. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jovicinac, we return. And I invite Mr. Krgovic to continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The documents you have are application of the international laws of war and Geneva Conventions. Can you look at Article 36? I said that it was L12. Page 21 in e-court, in English. And, for you, it's page 35. And it's tab 3 of the Zupljanin Defence material. Page 21 in Serbian in e-court. Mr. Jovicinac, 36, paragraph 3, it reads: "If it is established that a member of the armed forces of the SFRY," it has got to do with the SFRY, "the collected information and evidence shall be submitted to the military prosecutor directly or through the superior officer ..." So, Mr. Jovicinac, this applies to any member of the armed forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, according to the text, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at Article 38. The composition of the armed forces. And that's page 36 and page 21 in e-court. So it's the same page. Or, I'm sorry. It is - give me a moment, please - Article 48. Page 24 in English and Serbian in e-court. Under 1, where it speaks of the membership of the army, they enumerate various branches, and you'll see that they mention police units as well. According to these regulations, the commander of a military unit who is within his own AOR has the power to act upon all these various violations of international laws of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. But, you see, this area is prescribed by the Law on Military Courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, you will most certainly know that the supreme military prosecutor's office, precisely in order to avoid any confusion, laid down guide-lines for the work of military prosecutors' offices in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you, behind tab 19, document 2D10197.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, Mr. Jovicinac, again I would remind you to slow down and allow a gap between question and answer so the interpreters can keep up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D10197 doc ID for e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it is tab 19 -- or number 19 behind your tab. Let me read it out again. 2D10197. Doc ID. Sir, these are the guide-lines, issued by -- or, rather, forwarded by the VRS Main Staff to, among others, your military post in Banja Luka. As you see, it says that it's been received in Banja Luka on the 16th of October, 1992. Did you have an opportunity to see this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you turn the page, please. [In English] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There, Mr. Jovicinac, in the course of your work in 1992, did you come across this document?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us discuss some of the dilemmas we had and the differences of opinion. Let us now look at -- or, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to first give an explanation. The document that I showed to the witness consists of, to all extents and purposes, the cover letter and guide-lines which have already been admitted so I would like to go back to Stanisic's document, 1D368. So that's the document I'll be referring to, and that's behind tab 7 of the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, have a look, please, the relevant page is 15 in your binder; and for Their Honours, it's the English page 8 of the document. 1D368. Sir, have you found page 15?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The penultimate paragraph. The instructions from your superior organ read: "To all the commands of units which are duty-bound to investigate into all cases," and I say "all cases of war crime and within the area of their responsibility." Can you turn the page now, please.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I haven't found the portion you're reading. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Number 15. Oh, that's the number that is on that relevant page it's the typewritten number. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes, I have found the page. But the relevant text, I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: In order for the staff command to have -- to be fully apprised of the type and number of these crimes, all the commands of various units are duty-bound to engage in uncovering all sorts of war crimes, crimes against humanity and international laws of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the various territories that are within their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Next page, I think, is English 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Eight is on the screen, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may of assistance, in English it's page 8; and in Serbian, page 31 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is on the screen, Mr. Cvijetic. But could you point us to the relevant part of it? I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you scroll down. [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It starts at the bottom of the page and continues on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that's the page starting -- the paragraph starting with the words, "So that the command ..." Can we have the next page in English, please. We need page 9 in English. It reads -- well, it mentions all the various competencies of unit commanders, that they should inform the closest military police security and military judicial organs about any crimes they discover. Further down, Mr. Jovicinac, the penultimate paragraph which reads that the organs of the military police security organs and military judiciary organs will give priority in their work to these particular criminal offences so that the Main Staff and other relevant institutions would be notified as soon as possible and would be able to take measures within their competence, or within their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, it follows from these guide-lines that I've just read out that in a unit's area of responsibility of a given brigade commander, it is the commander and the military judiciary organs of that territory that are -- that have jurisdiction to be seized of all the various cases of war crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, let me just tell you this: Just by glancing at these pages, I can tell you that this is nothing new when it comes to the work of the military police and security organs and commanders. This procedure was used in all the different circumstances, and to tell you the truth, I wasn't aware of these instructions. That's number one. Number two: This does not release other organs from their obligation to work on the various war crimes and to bring charges for war crimes. When it comes to the army, of course, it is within the jurisdiction of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I, too, am slightly confused about this, because I'm not sure that I read out of this document the -- the -- the implications that you are mentioning to the witness. Isn't this about information, about providing information to the military authorities, including the military police, and the military courts about crimes? But from there, it doesn't follow necessarily that the military courts have to assume jurisdiction and try these cases, does it? Isn't this only about information?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. These are instructions. And if you look at the first couple of lines that I read out, you will see that it says there that they are duty-bound to work to uncover all manner of war crimes. And these are their work guide-lines. That's what the title says, after all. Moreover, the penultimate paragraph also states that judiciary organs and military police have to give priority to this sort of crime. This is an official document. There is only one other part that I will show to Mr. Jovicinac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please. Mr. Krgovic, if you read on in that paragraph, the text goes to say that the Main Staff and other competent institutions are notified as soon as possible. Which, again, suggest, at least to me, that the main purpose here is that no crime is left uncovered and -- but I'm not sure that this will necessarily imply that the military judicial organs automatically have jurisdiction over all crimes. I mean, that would literally sink the military courts, wouldn't it, if they would be seized of all crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you look at the paragraph in the middle, the third from the top, the last line makes it an obligation upon the military police to forward through the superior command of the military police the documentation they have gathered to the nearest military prosecutor's office as soon as may be, and from that point on, the military prosecutor would be seized of the case; of course, in application of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, my difficulty is that whereas, for your purposes, you may wish to engage the witness in a discussion on the effect of this document, the witness has said is he [indiscernible] so how --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: How far --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. I leave the topic. I just have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jovicinac, please revert to page 6 of these instructions, which would be page 4 in English in e-court, and page 13 in Serbian in e-court. The paragraph in the middle, Mr. Jovicinac, which is the third from the top in English. I will read only the relevant part of it: "The fact that a military recruit has not been listed in the military records is not something that matters. What matters is whether he has the military duty and failed to respond to a general call-up ..." So it isn't really necessary for a conscript to be listed in any of the military records, right? That's what arises from what I just read?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Please. Well, you see, the Law on Defence in the chapter regulating the work of the Secretariat of the Defence is duty-bound to provide information to all the conscripts -- on all the conscripts. Of course, it is possible that some of them would fall through the cracks but they would not be relieved or released from their military obligation. What is stated here is a reflection of the supreme military court's decision II K 676/66, which clarifies certain issues. But you see picking out a sentence here and there from the entire document is not going to lead us anywhere. If you look at the title of this document, they are guide-lines for defining the criteria of prosecution. For me, the criterion cannot be any sort of guide-lines, only the law. One can be held accountable for a crime only where this crime is envisaged under the law. So this does not involve the war crime; rather, it applies to a number of criminal offences that the army was burdened with in that period of time. This is what I can tell you after having glanced, like avoiding military service, Article 214. And for your information, there were many such criminal reports based on this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't have much time. My time is limited. I'm sorry to interrupt you and I see Mr. Olmsted is on his feet. So you, sir, when it comes to this document and to the case law of the supreme military court about people in the military records and the need for them to be in the military records, you don't know about this and you haven't seen that; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: No. I speak on the basis of the fact that it is the duty of all citizens --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be fair to the witness and to be -- not to mislead this Trial Chamber, the paragraph you were referring to starts out saying where certain documents aren't available, that they haven't been kept properly. In those circumstances, then you can resort to this situation where perhaps you don't need to have Vob 8 or some other form of registry. So I think it is misleading to this witness to suggest that there doesn't have to be documentation of a person's military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when it comes to that, when it comes to the records, it is debatable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, would you allow me a follow-up question to that. Mr. Jovicinac, can you explain to me what a general call-up means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General call-up or general mobilisation means that the competent state organ who is authorised to announce the general mobilisation due to the urgency and the threat posed to the country -- means that all those who are fit for military service and who have their war-time assignment, be it in the police or be it in the civilian defence, have to respond. And those who do not have their war-time assignments and are fit for military service, also have to respond. Those who are not fit for military service are entitled to respond as well, but they need to undergo certain procedure; medical examinations, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So general call-up is a mobilisation of people who, due to that mobilisation, become soldiers. Simply said. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And when I say "people," I could, as well, have said conscripts. Conscripts become effective soldiers by a mobilisation order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By responding and going to their units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course. Now, if a police unit consisting of people that are not in the military at that moment, that are not mobilised, if such a unit is resubordinated, would you call that a mobilisation or a general call-up, due to a general call-up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I haven't quite understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let me put it in another way. This paragraph that was read to you about the fact that the -- I read the last sentences: "What is important is the fact that he has a military obligation and that he has failed to respond to general call-up." Okay. My question is: The situation of resubordination of a unit of policemen, does that correspond to what is called a mobilisation or general call-up, or is that something different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All persons who have their war-time assignment in the police, when there is a general mobilisation call-up, they have to report to the unit to which they have been assigned. They're duty-bound to respond in accordance with their war-time assignment. They cannot simply say, I will remain in police and go and report to police. They can only go to police if they had previously been given a war-time assignment in police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But that's what I mean. People who have been given a war-time assignment within the police. And being within the police, being within a certain police unit, this unit, at a certain point in time, for a short time, is resubordinated to the military for combat reasons. Would you then say that those policemen were in the military due to mobilisation or due to a general call-up? Or would you say they were temporarily there due to a resubordination order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my belief that, pursuant to a competent organ's order, they are resubordinated to the superior command. They -- there must be an order stating that a civilian police unit is being resubordinated to a military command. It doesn't happen just on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, at the moment when the general mobilisation is being declared in the period of immediate threat of war, all citizens fit for military service become conscripts; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I don't know. You keep insisting on one thing all the time. I have already responded to this. I've already replied to that question. In an orderly society, all military conscripts are aware of their war-time assignment, and you know this full well. They have to report to their commands, to their units. They cannot pick and choose where they will report. They have to report to where their war-time assignment is. Those who do not have such an assignment, they have to report to the Secretariat for National Defence to get their assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. You did not reply to my question. My question was very clear. When an immediate threat of war is declared, when the general mobilisation is declared, all citizens fit for military service become conscripts and are duty-bound to report in accordance with their war-time assignments; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes. And in accordance with the law, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I would remind you that collectively you have 37 minutes left. Between the two of you, you have 37 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just one topic in relation to the document tendered to Mr. Olmsted, so I would kindly ask for additional five minutes to deal with that -- these two documents, the list of police and soldiers. Whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, when the Prosecutor showed you the lists with persons who were first put on the police lists, and then later on, a month or so later, they were put on the military police unit's lists, if somebody were to leave their position, then the competent command would initiate proceedings to change their war-time assignment so that instead of being assigned to the police units, they would be sent to the military units of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, I can't really answer that question. I don't know whether you're referring to the military police or civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Removing civilian police from the war-time assignment, according to what I know, would mean that only the competent MUP organisation could remove them from a war-time assignment. It is a very complicated procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. Would you agree with me that the command of the brigade to which that unit belongs would propose and initiate the proceedings to remove them?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: That doesn't need to be necessarily the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 2D07-1154 doc ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which is tab 16 in your binder, Zupljanin Defence binder. Here, Mr. Jovicinac, this is a police brigade that was in Orasija [phoen], and they sent their regular combat report to the command of the East Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the text. After the introductory part it will be the middle paragraph, the underlined paragraph. Do you see that where it says: "During the day, the 3rd Battalion and the 4th Company of the 3rd Battalion abandoned their positions. It was proposed that reserve policemen be taken off the war-time assignment of the police and be put at the disposal of the Secretariats of National Defence of their home municipalities, with a request that they be immediately made available to the VRS war-time units."

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Sir, I have already replied to this. This a police brigade not a military brigade, and they are entitled to initiate something of this sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you turn to the second page and see who the commander of this brigade is?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: You know what? I can't really go into who signed what. I can just see what it says at the top. It says the police brigade, general security services.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says here that it was signed by Bosko Peulic, a colonel.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who Bosko Peulic is and whether he commanded that brigade. If this was indeed a police brigade, then they had their own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is precisely the commander who is proposing -- I apologise. Please look at whom the police brigade is proposing this. They are proposing this to the Command of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: You know what? I'm now going into issues that I'm not fully familiar with, and they could make matters more complicated. I would rather not comment on this. I think that this is yet another example of many things that I have seen here that were not done in accordance with the law. This command is not competent to make such proposals to the commander of the corps. Since this is a police brigade based on what I believe, they are only competent --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you cannot give us a clear answer then please do not speculate, so if you cannot give a precise answer --

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you what the law says, what the law provisions say. I'm not speculating. I apologise. My answer was that the police cannot be removed from war-time assignment by whoever wanted to do so. There was a procedure that regulated that. I apologise for going fast. The proposal had to be sent to the competent organ with a list of persons, and then an order had to be issued for these people to be sent to the Secretariat of National Defence who would then, in turn, reassign them to other units. That was the law specified procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we have touched upon this, the law also said that if somebody was accused for a war crime carrying with it a prison sentence of more than five years, such a person had to be put in detention; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the military prosecutor's office, in all such cases, agreed that detention be -- that these people be released from detention; right?

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P1284.38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which is your tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I inquire whether this is relevant to one of the topics? This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't see how this deals with resubordinated police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jovicinac, have you found the document? You personally here violated this law that you're invoking now by releasing from detention people who had committed heinous crimes in Velegica.

utterances.speaker: SRBOLJUB JOVICINAC
utterances.text: Listen, a military prosecutor can give a proposal, and if it is relevant to explain why I did what I did here, then I will do that.
